sdlc-foundations.hint: First sort into a family — development philosophy, process-maturity rating, testing technique, or code-level vulnerability class — then land on the specific term inside that family.
sdlc-foundations.note: This board covers Domain 8's process, maturity, testing, and vulnerability-vocabulary layer. Acquisition-risk questions (COTS, open source, third-party, managed/cloud services) and single-language secure-coding mechanics live in a different game.
sdlc-foundations.zones[0].def: A linear SDLC where each phase — requirements, design, build, test, operate — must fully close before the next opens, with no built-in path back once a gate is passed. Pick this when a scene stresses requirements frozen up front and sequential sign-off, not iterative re-planning (Agile) and not a score of how mature the org's process is (Maturity models).
sdlc-foundations.zones[1].def: Iterative, incremental delivery built around short cycles of planning, building and evaluating, with frequent stakeholder feedback and self-organizing teams reprioritizing as they go. Pick this when the scene is about adapting scope mid-project and shipping working slices often — the discriminator against DevSecOps is that this zone is about the planning/delivery cadence itself, not the automated security tooling fused into a pipeline.
sdlc-foundations.zones[2].def: Extends a DevOps CI/CD pipeline by embedding security controls — scanning gates, policy-as-code, threat-modeling checkpoints — directly into the automated build-and-release cycle instead of checking security at the end. Pick this when a scene shows security folded into the automated pipeline alongside ops; a single named technique running inside that pipeline (SAST, DAST) still sorts to its own zone, not here.
sdlc-foundations.zones[3].def: Frameworks that score how consistent and repeatable an organization's software or security *process* is — CMM's five levels (Initial through Optimizing) for general software-process discipline, SAMM's five business functions for security-practice maturity — rather than telling a team which SDLC methodology to run. Pick this when the scene is an assessor rating an org's process capability, not a team choosing or executing a specific methodology.
sdlc-foundations.zones[4].def: Static analysis of source or intermediate code without executing it, usually pre-compile, catching flaws like unreachable branches or policy violations at the code level. Pick this when the scene examines code at rest before it ever runs — not a running application (DAST) and not code being hit with malformed live input (Fuzzing).
sdlc-foundations.zones[5].def: Dynamic evaluation of a program while it is running, driving the live application to surface exploitable behavior — logic errors, memory leaks, session handling flaws — without needing source-code access. Pick this when the scene exercises the running app as a black box with realistic, well-formed traffic — the discriminator against Fuzzing is that Fuzzing narrows in on deliberately malformed or random input specifically.
sdlc-foundations.zones[6].def: An automated technique that bombards a running program with malformed, random or boundary-pushing input at an interface, hunting for a crash or unhandled path that exposes an exploitable defect. Pick this when the scene centers on injecting deliberately corrupted or oversized data — a narrower, input-focused subset of dynamic testing, distinct from DAST's broader behavioral sweep and from a human-led Penetration test.
sdlc-foundations.zones[7].def: An authorized, human-led simulated attack against a live target, chaining findings — including automated-scan output — toward a defined objective under agreed rules of engagement. Pick this when a person is exercising attacker judgment and pursuing a goal, not an unattended automated tool running a sweep (DAST) or a fuzz harness (Fuzzing).
sdlc-foundations.zones[8].def: Untrusted data reaching an interpreter — SQL, LDAP, OS command — as part of a query or command because input was never separated from code, letting the interpreter execute something unintended. Pick this when unsanitized input flows straight into a query/command engine, not when the failure is a missing permission check on an otherwise-valid request (Broken access control).
sdlc-foundations.zones[9].def: Failures that let an authenticated user act outside their intended permissions — reading or modifying another user's data, or reaching admin functions — because the server never re-checks authorization on the specific object requested. Pick this when the request itself is well-formed and the user is logged in, but the ownership/permission check is missing — not an unhardened default setting exposing the same data (Security misconfiguration), and not input reaching an interpreter (Injection).
sdlc-foundations.zones[10].def: Insecure default settings, unnecessary exposed features, verbose error output, or missing hardening anywhere in the stack — a setting problem, not a code-logic one. Pick this when the root cause is what was left configured or exposed by default, distinct from a code-level authorization gap (Broken access control) and from an interpreter receiving unsanitized input (Injection).

sdlf-01.label: A municipal payroll rewrite locks every requirement at kickoff; the team can only start design once every requirement doc is signed off, and reopening requirements later needs a formal change board.
sdlf-01.sub: Which SDLC model is in play?
sdlf-01.why: Sequential, gated phases with requirements frozen before design begins is Waterfall's signature; the tempting neighbour is a maturity model, but this scene is about the methodology itself, not a score of how disciplined the org's process is.

sdlf-02.label: A defense contractor's statement of work requires preliminary design and detailed design to be delivered and signed as two separate, sequential stage-gates before any code is written.
sdlf-02.sub: Which SDLC model is in play?
sdlf-02.why: Discrete, ordered stage-gates that must close before the next opens is the linear model, not the short-cycle re-planning of Agile or the automated pipeline gating of DevSecOps.

sdlf-03.label: A fintech squad ships a working slice of the loan-approval feature every two weeks and re-prioritizes the backlog after each demo based on live customer feedback.
sdlf-03.sub: Which SDLC model is in play?
sdlf-03.why: Short iterations with reprioritization driven by fresh feedback is Agile's core loop, distinct from Waterfall's frozen up-front scope and from DevSecOps, whose distinguishing trait is security tooling fused into the automated pipeline, not the planning cadence itself.

sdlf-04.label: Product owners and developers hold a daily quarter-hour sync to reset that sprint's priorities as market conditions shift mid-project.
sdlf-04.sub: Which SDLC model is in play?
sdlf-04.why: Daily replanning in response to changing conditions is the iterative planning cadence itself — no security-scanning or pipeline automation is described, which is what would push it toward DevSecOps instead.

sdlf-05.label: A retailer's pipeline chains secret-scanning, dependency-vulnerability checks and a container-policy gate, all running automatically on every merge before a human reviewer even opens the pull request.
sdlf-05.sub: Which SDLC model is in play?
sdlf-05.why: Multiple security disciplines woven into the automated build pipeline is the DevSecOps philosophy; a single one of those checks in isolation would name its own technique (SAST), but the chained, pipeline-wide integration is the tell here.

sdlf-06.label: Security engineers add a threat-modeling checkpoint to each sprint's Definition of Done, running alongside the same automation that deploys the build to production.
sdlf-06.sub: Which SDLC model is in play?
sdlf-06.why: Security review embedded into the same automated cadence that operations uses to deploy is DevSecOps's fusion; Agile alone would only describe the sprint cadence, without security controls riding along inside the deployment automation.

sdlf-07.label: An assessor rates a software house at 'basic project planning and configuration management now exist, but there's still no organization-wide standard process.'
sdlf-07.why: Scoring an org's process discipline on a defined level scale is what a maturity model does; the org isn't choosing between Waterfall and Agile here, it's being graded on how consistently it already runs whichever one it uses.

sdlf-08.label: A security review maps a vendor's practices against five named business functions — governance, design, implementation, verification, operations — and scores each on a maturity scale.
sdlf-08.why: Scoring security practice against named business functions is SAMM's structure; it's still a maturity-assessment framework, not the DevSecOps pipeline it might later recommend implementing.

sdlf-09.label: A tool parses an application's source before it is ever compiled and flags an unreachable code branch plus a mismatched data-type assignment.
sdlf-09.why: Examining code without executing it, pre-compile, is static analysis; the same flaw found by exercising a running instance instead would be DAST's territory.

sdlf-10.label: Every pull request automatically triggers a scan of just the changed lines for hard-coded credentials and unsafe string concatenation, before a human reviewer opens the diff.
sdlf-10.why: An automated scan of source text itself, run before execution, is the static technique; running it inside a broader pipeline of chained security gates would be described as DevSecOps, but this item names one specific scan.

sdlf-11.label: Testers drive a live checkout service with realistic HTTP requests, watching for exposed session tokens and memory leaks, with no access to its source code.
sdlf-11.why: Exercising a running application as a black box with well-formed traffic is dynamic testing; the lack of source access is exactly what separates it from SAST, and the traffic being realistic rather than deliberately corrupted separates it from Fuzzing.

sdlf-12.label: A nightly job replays a scripted, valid user journey against staging to see whether a newly deployed rule quietly lets requests bypass the rate limiter.
sdlf-12.why: A scripted but legitimate interaction sequence run against the live app is dynamic testing's behavioral sweep, not a static code review and not a fuzz harness generating malformed data.

sdlf-13.label: A harness feeds an image-parsing library thousands of randomly corrupted file headers overnight, looking for the crash that reveals a buffer overflow.
sdlf-13.why: Deliberately malformed, randomly generated input aimed at one interface is fuzzing's narrow focus; a broader behavioral test with realistic, valid traffic against the whole running app would be DAST instead.

sdlf-14.label: An API gateway is bombarded with automatically generated oversized and boundary-value payloads, hunting for an unhandled exception path.
sdlf-14.why: Automated generation of boundary-pushing, malformed payloads is fuzzing; a human deliberately chaining that finding toward a further objective would shift the scene to Penetration testing.

sdlf-15.label: A hired red-team operator chains a phishing foothold with a misconfigured file share to reach the domain controller, working under a signed rules-of-engagement letter.
sdlf-15.why: A human exercising attacker judgment to chain footholds toward a domain-controller objective, under agreed scope, is a penetration test; an unattended automated scan producing the same initial finding would be DAST or Fuzzing instead.

sdlf-16.label: After the automated scanner's report lands, a tester manually verifies which findings are actually exploitable and pivots from one weak host to a more sensitive second one.
sdlf-16.why: Manual verification and pivoting toward a further target is the human-led exploitation phase that follows automated scanning, not the automated scan itself, which only produced the raw list of findings.

sdlf-17.label: A search box passes user text straight into a backend SQL WHERE clause with no parameterization, letting an attacker retrieve every customer's record in one query.
sdlf-17.sub: Which OWASP vulnerability class is this?
sdlf-17.why: Untrusted input reaching a query engine unseparated from the command itself is the defining pattern of injection; the request was authenticated normally, which rules out a missing-permission-check story (Broken access control).

sdlf-18.label: A directory-lookup widget concatenates a submitted username straight into an LDAP filter string, letting an attacker widen the filter to return every employee's record.
sdlf-18.sub: Which OWASP vulnerability class is this?
sdlf-18.why: Unsanitized input reaching an interpreter — here an LDAP filter rather than SQL — is still injection; no default setting or missing ownership check is described, which rules out Security misconfiguration and Broken access control.

sdlf-19.label: A logged-in customer edits the order ID in the URL and successfully views another customer's invoice, because the server never re-checks who owns that order before returning it.
sdlf-19.sub: Which OWASP vulnerability class is this?
sdlf-19.why: The request is well-formed and the user is properly authenticated; the failure is a missing ownership check on the specific object requested, not an interpreter executing manipulated input (Injection) and not an exposed default setting (Security misconfiguration).

sdlf-20.label: An API's report-download endpoint accepts any report ID in the request body, and the server never verifies the requesting user actually owns that report before returning it.
sdlf-20.sub: Which OWASP vulnerability class is this?
sdlf-20.why: A missing per-object authorization check on an otherwise valid, authenticated request is broken access control; the endpoint itself works exactly as configured, so this isn't a hardening gap (Security misconfiguration).

sdlf-21.label: A cloud storage bucket is left with public-read permissions because the team never changed the platform's default access setting before go-live.
sdlf-21.sub: Which OWASP vulnerability class is this?
sdlf-21.why: An unhardened default left in place is a configuration problem, not a code-level flaw; no query engine or authorization check is involved, which rules out Injection and Broken access control.

sdlf-22.label: An application server still returns verbose stack-trace error pages in production, revealing internal file paths and library versions to anyone who trips an exception.
sdlf-22.sub: Which OWASP vulnerability class is this?
sdlf-22.why: Exposed debug output that should have been disabled for production is a settings failure across the stack, distinct from a missing per-object permission check (Broken access control) or unsanitized input reaching an interpreter (Injection).
